tldr: By representing the environment with a sparse 3D skeleton connecting robot joints with object centers and interaction points, SkeleWAM co-learns action generation and future skeleton prediction. With only 57.1M parameters, this compact model achieves an 85.9% success rate on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, outperforming Cosmos-Policy.
hero_caption: A comparison between conventional, computationally heavy video/latent prediction and SkeleWAM's sparse 3D skeleton approach. By extracting skeletons from RGB-D observations and robot proprioception, and using future skeleton prediction as auxiliary supervision during training, SkeleWAM balances high task success with fast, memory-efficient inference.
overview:
When robots autonomously plan and execute tasks, world-action models (WAMs) that predict how the world changes in response to robot actions have gained significant attention. However, most existing WAMs predict future states as raw video frames or high-dimensional visual latent representations. These approaches are computationally expensive and retain task-irrelevant visual details like color and background, obscuring the essential geometric relationships between the robot and objects.

To address this, the authors hypothesized that manipulation primarily requires sparse 3D geometric information composed of robot joints and object interaction points. The proposed method, SkeleWAM, constructs a sparse 3D skeleton online from RGB-D observations and robot proprioception, using it as a unified geometric state space. During training, the model performs multi-task learning for action generation and future skeleton prediction, leveraging geometric dynamics prediction as an auxiliary supervisory signal for action learning. At inference time, the future prediction branch is discarded, generating actions directly from the current skeleton and language instruction. In addition, the authors introduce Medoid Action Consensus (MAC), a lightweight consensus mechanism that reduces the variance of stochastic action sampling.

SkeleWAM was evaluated on the large-scale simulator benchmark LIBERO-Plus—which includes perturbations across viewpoints, backgrounds, and layouts—as well as on real-world manipulation tasks. Despite having only 57.1M parameters, SkeleWAM achieved an 85.9% success rate, surpassing the much larger Cosmos-Policy and demonstrating remarkable robustness against camera viewpoint shifts. This work clearly demonstrates the effectiveness of explicitly modeling the geometric structures essential for robot control.
contributions: Formulation of world-action modeling using a unified sparse 3D skeleton state space composed of robot joints, object centers, and interaction points.

Introduction of SkeleWAM, a compact model that uses future skeleton prediction as auxiliary geometric supervision without requiring visual reconstruction, discarding the prediction branch at inference for fast execution.

Introduction of Medoid Action Consensus (MAC), a strategy that stably selects a representative trajectory close to the medoid among multiple sampled action candidates without requiring reward models or trajectory averaging.
Demonstration of superior zero-shot robustness and parameter efficiency over existing large VLAs and world model approaches on the large-scale LIBERO-Plus benchmark and real-world experiments.

sections.heading: Ditching Pixels for Skeletons: Why Sparse Geometry Matters
sections.summary: Existing world-action models predict videos or latent features, incurring high computational costs and obscuring task-critical geometric relationships. SkeleWAM addresses this by representing the scene as a sparse 3D skeleton connecting robot joints and object interaction points, achieving high robustness with a lightweight model.
sections.details:
In recent years, methods like ACT and Diffusion Policy, as well as large-scale Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models such as RT-2 and $\pi_{0}$, have achieved remarkable results. Moving one step further, world-action models (WAMs) that jointly learn robot action generation and future state prediction have been actively studied.

However, existing WAMs face significant hurdles. Prevailing methods predict future states as high-resolution videos or latent vectors from learned visual encoders, requiring immense computational resources. Furthermore, pixels and latent spaces retain appearance information unrelated to control, such as lighting and textures, failing to explicitly expose the fundamental geometric structure: the relative positions and contact states between the robot and objects.

The authors realized that essential manipulation information can be compactly represented by a sparse 3D skeleton (landmarks) of the robot and objects. The state space is defined as a graph where nodes correspond to robot joint positions, target object centers, and interaction points (such as grasp candidates). This unified skeleton allows the model to efficiently co-learn action generation and future state prediction without spending computational power on visual reconstruction.

Despite having only 57.1M parameters, SkeleWAM achieved an overall success rate of 85.9% on the LIBERO-Plus benchmark, outperforming the strong baseline Cosmos-Policy by 3.7 percentage points. It demonstrated exceptional robustness against camera viewpoint perturbations, scoring 93.4% and outpacing Cosmos-Policy by 17.6 percentage points.

captions.F1: Comparison between dense world prediction models and SkeleWAM. Instead of predicting the future of pixels or dense point clouds, SkeleWAM models only the 3D skeleton linking key robot and object points, dramatically reducing model parameters and computation while achieving high success rates.

sections.heading: From Visuomotor Policies to World Models: A Shift Toward Explicit Geometry
sections.summary: Visuomotor policies and VLAs optimize action generation alone without modeling environment transitions. While existing world models implicitly encode geometry through videos or latent features, SkeleWAM directly operates in an explicit geometric state space using 3D skeletons.
sections.details:
### 2.1 Visuomotor Policies and VLA Models
Robot manipulation has largely advanced through end-to-end learning that maps observation images directly to actions. ACT predicts temporally consistent action chunks, while Diffusion Policy and DP3 model expressive action distributions using 2D images and 3D point clouds, respectively. Furthermore, generalist foundation models following language instructions, such as RT-2, OpenVLA, and flow-matching-based models like $\pi_{0}$ and $\pi_{0.5}$, have emerged. However, these methods only optimize direct observation-to-action mappings without explicitly learning the dynamics of how objects and environments transition in response to actions.

### 2.2 World-Action Models (WAMs)
To capture environment transitions, WAMs that simultaneously predict actions and future states have gained traction. Approaches like WorldVLA and Cosmos-Policy leverage video generation models, VLA-JEPA avoids pixel reconstruction by predicting latent features, and Fast-WAM uses video prediction as an auxiliary training task and discards it during inference.

However, videos and visual latents represent interaction geometry only implicitly. Latent representations are dictated by image encoder training objectives, retaining appearance details. In contrast, SkeleWAM defines both current and future states as explicit geometric parameters: sparse 3D skeletons. By leveraging future geometric change prediction as an auxiliary supervisor, it acquires strong geometric representations without performing any visual reconstruction, setting it apart from existing works.

sections.heading: From Skeleton Extraction to Flow Prediction and MAC: How SkeleWAM Works
sections.summary: SkeleWAM extracts a 3D skeleton from RGB-D inputs and forward kinematics, then predicts flow via a two-branch transformer consisting of World and Action Experts. At inference, future prediction is dropped, and Medoid Action Consensus (MAC) selects the central trajectory among multiple candidates for stable control.
sections.details:
### 3.1 Problem Formulation
Given a language instruction $\ell$, RGB-D observation $o_t$, and robot proprioception $q_t$ (such as joint angles), the model generates an action chunk $\mathbf{A}_t$ spanning future $H_a$ steps. In this work, the scene is represented as a sparse 3D skeleton $\mathbf{S}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N \times 3}$ with $N$ nodes. During training, the model also predicts a future skeleton sequence $\mathbf{S}^+_t$ over $H_s$ steps.

### 3.2 Skeleton-based World Representation
The scene skeleton consists of robot keypoints $\mathbf{J}_t \in \mathbb{R}^{N_r \times 3}$ (joint and end-effector positions) and object landmarks $\mathbf{O}_{t,m}$. Each object is represented by its center and interaction points (points relevant to grasping or contact). Robot joint coordinates are calculated accurately via forward kinematics (FK), while object landmarks are estimated from RGB-D point clouds using a frozen pre-trained vision perception network. All points are transformed and normalized into a shared robot-centric coordinate frame.

### 3.3 Network Architecture
The language instruction, current skeleton, noisy action chunk, and noisy future skeleton sequence are tokenized. Following the Fast-WAM design, the architecture consists of two branches: a World Expert and an Action Expert. A block-attention mask ensures that action prediction tokens and future skeleton prediction tokens do not cross-attend to each other; both only attend to the current skeleton tokens.

### 3.4 Training with Flow Matching
Flow matching is adopted for both action generation and future skeleton prediction. The target vector fields are trained as linear interpolations between standard Gaussian noise and ground-truth trajectories, minimizing the sum of an action loss and a skeleton loss. Because both losses backpropagate through the current skeleton tokens, the future prediction task strongly guides the geometric representation learning of the World Expert.

### 3.5 Inference and Medoid Action Consensus (MAC)
To minimize inference overhead, future skeleton tokens are omitted completely. The model generates actions by integrating the action vector field over 10 steps using only the current skeleton and instruction. To mitigate stochastic sampling variance, the authors introduce Medoid Action Consensus (MAC). It samples $K$ action candidates (default $K=3$) from independent noise and selects the candidate with the smallest average distance to the others across continuous action dimensions over the initial $h$ steps. MAC does not require a learned reward model and avoids the risk of trajectory averaging causing unnatural or invalid motions.

captions.F2: The overall SkeleWAM pipeline. On the left, a sparse 3D skeleton is extracted from RGB-D and robot proprioception. In the top right, a transformer jointly learns actions and future skeletons. During inference (bottom right), future prediction is omitted, and MAC selects the optimal trajectory among multiple action candidates.

sections.heading: Surpassing Giant Models with 57M Parameters: Simulator and Real-World Results
sections.summary: Evaluated across 10,030 perturbation environments in LIBERO-Plus, SkeleWAM achieved an 85.9% success rate, beating Cosmos-Policy. It also reached an 89% average success rate on real-world robot arm tasks, with ablation studies confirming the necessity of interaction points and future skeleton supervision.
sections.details:
### 4.1 Simulation Setup
Evaluations were conducted on LIBERO-Plus across 10,030 variants spanning seven perturbation types: viewpoints, backgrounds, language, layouts, and noise. Zero-shot performance was measured without fine-tuning on the perturbed test environments. SkeleWAM was compared against state-of-the-art VLAs like OpenVLA and $\pi_{0.5}$, as well as world model approaches such as Cosmos-Policy and Fast-WAM.

### 4.2 Simulation Results
- **Zero-Shot Robustness**: SkeleWAM achieved an overall success rate of 85.9%, outperforming the strongest observation-based baseline, Cosmos-Policy (82.2%), by 3.7 percentage points. Under camera viewpoint perturbations, it reached 93.4%, outperforming Cosmos-Policy (75.8%) by 17.6 points. It was also highly resilient to background (96.0%) and noise (93.9%) changes. By explicitly operating in 3D robot coordinates, the model remains unperturbed by camera shifts and visual variations.
- **Comparison with Privileged Information (sim-state)**: The privileged variant, SkeleWAM (sim-state), which extracts 3D coordinates directly from the simulator, achieved 87.7%—only 1.8 points higher than the observation-based version. This confirms that RGB-D skeleton extraction is sufficiently accurate for practical control.
- **Challenges in Layout Perturbations**: Under extreme initial object layout changes, performance dropped to 66.6%, trailing behind $\pi_{0.5}$ (84.1%). Since the privileged sim-state version only achieved 69.0%, this bottleneck stems from the difficulty of generalizing to unseen spatial arrangements using sparse geometry alone, rather than perceptual errors.

### 4.3 Real-World Experiments
Using an ARX R5 robot arm and RealSense cameras, five manipulation tasks (opening a drawer, putting a block in a drawer, stacking bowls, etc.) were conducted with 20 trials each. SkeleWAM achieved an average success rate of 89%, outperforming Cosmos-Policy (87%), Fast-WAM (83%), and $\pi_{0.5}$ (76%).

### 4.4 Ablation Studies
- **Skeleton Components**: Using only object centers dropped success to 82.3%, and using only interaction points dropped it to 77.7%, compared to 85.9% with both. Positional references and contact points are both essential.
- **Auxiliary Value of Future Prediction**: Removing the future skeleton prediction task during training caused success to plunge by 5.8 points to 80.1%. Even if discarded at inference, future prediction plays a crucial role in representation learning.
- **MAC Design**: Sampling $K=3$ candidates yielded 85.9%, a clear boost over single sampling ($K=1$, 84.2%). Increasing candidates to 5 or 10 plateaued performance (85.2%, 84.1%), making $K=3$ the optimal tradeoff between compute and accuracy.

sections.heading: Summary and Future Outlook: Geometric World Models for Efficient Robot Control
sections.summary: SkeleWAM demonstrates that 3D skeletons provide a promising new direction for world models, combining parameter efficiency with viewpoint robustness. Addressing remaining challenges like extreme layout changes will require uncertainty-aware perception and adaptive landmark designs.
sections.details:
This study introduced SkeleWAM, a compact world-action model that uses sparse 3D skeletons composed of robot joints and object interaction points as environmental states. By co-training action generation and future skeleton prediction using flow matching, the model learns rich geometric representations while bypassing heavy image reconstruction. Furthermore, the lightweight MAC mechanism stabilizes inference rollouts.

Evaluations on LIBERO-Plus and real-world hardware confirmed that a compact 57.1M model can achieve greater robustness against viewpoint shifts and background noise than billion-parameter VLAs or video-based WAMs.

However, generalizing to radically altered spatial layouts remains an open challenge. For future work, the authors plan to incorporate perception uncertainty, task-adaptive interaction point selection, and richer relational structures between objects, aiming to further boost generalization while preserving skeleton simplicity.

takeaways: Predicting the future of a sparse 3D skeleton as an auxiliary task provides sufficient geometric supervision for action learning, eliminating the need to predict pixels or latents.
Explicitly representing state in a robot-centric 3D geometric space delivers remarkable zero-shot robustness against camera viewpoint and background changes.
Stochastic sampling variance inherent to diffusion and flow matching can be easily mitigated using medoid-based trajectory selection (MAC) without requiring a learned reward model.
limitations: Success rates drop to 66.6% under significant object layout perturbations, falling short of massive VLAs like $\pi_{0.5}$ pre-trained on extensive datasets.
Relying on a fixed, external pre-trained vision model for object landmark detection makes the system vulnerable to novel, unseen objects or severe occlusions.
Object interaction points are determined statically or heuristically, lacking a mechanism to adaptively redefine landmarks for deformable or highly complex objects.
